title: Morris v. Sparrow
summary: A horse that the claimant had personally trained had sufficiently distinctive value to justify delivery of that horse rather than an award of its market price.
notes:
Court: Supreme Court of Arkansas (1956).

The decision is Morris v. Sparrow, 225 Ark. 1019, 287 S.W.2d 583 (1956); Morris refused to deliver Keno on the ground that Sparrow had not done a good job, and the court's rule is that equity may order specific performance of a contract for a chattel when the chattel is unique or damages would be inadequate.

sections.Parties: Archie Sparrow, a cowboy and horse trainer, sought specific performance against Morris, the ranch owner who allegedly promised him a horse as part of his compensation.
sections.Material Facts:
The parties initially planned travel together, then arranged for Sparrow to remain at Morris’s Arkansas ranch while Morris went to Canada. They agreed on 16 weeks of ranch work for $400. Sparrow testified that he was also to receive Keno, a brown horse. Morris maintained that delivery of the horse depended on satisfactory ranch work and that Sparrow had failed to satisfy that condition.

Keno was practically unbroken when Sparrow arrived. During spare time, Sparrow trained the horse so that it was close to becoming a first-class roping horse. Morris paid the monetary compensation but did not deliver Keno. Sparrow’s own work with this particular animal made an ordinary market replacement an inadequate equivalent.
sections.Procedural History: The chancery court ordered delivery of the horse. On appeal, the Supreme Court of Arkansas affirmed both the availability of specific performance and the trial court’s resolution of the dispute over Sparrow’s entitlement.
sections.Issue: Could a court specifically enforce an agreement concerning personal property, and did the factual dispute about satisfactory work defeat Sparrow’s entitlement to Keno?
sections.Holding: Specific performance was available because of the horse’s special and peculiar value to Sparrow. The court declined to disturb the chancellor’s finding in his favor on entitlement.
sections.Reasoning:
The general reluctance to compel delivery of ordinary goods rests on the adequacy of money damages. Here, the claimant had transformed an unbroken animal through his own training. The resulting horse had a distinctive value to him that a market-price award would not adequately replace. The court therefore treated the case as an exception to the usual approach to personal property.

The alleged satisfaction condition presented a separate factual question. Both parties testified before the chancellor, who was better placed to evaluate their evidence. The appellate court could not say that the finding for Sparrow was against the preponderance of the evidence. The opinion does not articulate the same detailed satisfaction-standard analysis later encountered in Mattei or Gibson; those are useful comparisons rather than additional holdings of Morris.

priorVersions.summary: A trained horse could warrant specific performance because ordinary money damages would not adequately replace that particular horse.
priorVersions.notes:
Court: Supreme Court of Arkansas (1956).

Read with the specific-relief notes on Curtice Brothers, personal services, and negative injunctions. A label such as “goods” does not by itself resolve adequacy of damages.

sections.Parties: Sparrow, a cowboy and rodeo performer, sought the horse Keno from Morris, for whom he had worked.
sections.Material Facts: The arrangement involved sixteen weeks of ranch work, $400, and the horse. Sparrow trained Keno in his spare time. Morris contested whether Sparrow had performed satisfactorily, but the trial court credited Sparrow’s account.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court ordered delivery of the horse. The Supreme Court of Arkansas affirmed the decree of specific performance.
sections.Issue: Was a particular horse sufficiently distinctive, and Sparrow’s performance sufficient, to justify specific performance rather than money damages?
sections.Holding: The decree was upheld. The court accepted the trial court’s resolution of the factual dispute over performance and regarded the trained horse as having a special value not adequately represented by an ordinary damages award.
sections.Reasoning: Specific performance responds to the inadequacy of substitution in money. Sparrow’s training of the horse and its suitability for his rodeo use supported the decree. The case concerns transfer of property, not an order forcing a person to provide services. The surrounding notes extend the inquiry to an animal’s sentimental value and to goods for which an apparently ordinary market cannot supply the required quantity or timing.

learning.why: The case makes the adequacy of a substitute concrete. A thing’s market price and its value to the party who contracted for it can diverge.

topics.specific-performance: Personal training made the identified horse difficult to replace with money.
topics.conditions: Morris disputed whether the agreed performance condition had been met.
topics.discretion: The alleged satisfaction term provides a comparison with the later satisfaction-clause cases.
topics.satisfaction: Morris defended on the ground that delivery of the horse was conditioned on his satisfaction with Sparrow's ranch work, a satisfaction-condition argument the chancellor rejected on the facts.
